quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Every summer, dry grass on the hills above Ojai turns into fuel for wildfires. Crews used to cut it by machine, which was noisy and expensive. This year the town hired a herd of goats instead. The animals eat the brush down to bare soil in a few days, and they need only water and a fence. Fire officials say the approach costs about half as much and leaves the hillsides quieter.
options: Goats offer a cheaper, quieter way to reduce wildfire fuel.
Machines cut brush faster than goats, so officials avoid animals.
The town bought goats to produce milk for local residents.
The town's fire crews now train goats to clear brush on the steep slopes.
quests.correctAnswer: Goats offer a cheaper, quieter way to reduce wildfire fuel.
quests.hint: Decide what the goats are compared with before you judge the options.
quests.explanation: The paragraph presents goats as an alternative to noisy, costly machines for clearing fuel. The wrong options overstate the change, reverse the speed comparison or invent a purpose.
keyPoints: Dry grass around Ojai becomes wildfire fuel each summer.
Goats now clear the brush instead of noisy machines.
Officials say the method costs about half as much and is quieter.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Patients on the fourth-floor ward rarely slept well. Monitors beeped, trolleys rattled and staff talked loudly at the desk. A nurse suggested measuring the noise, and the readings were often as high as a busy street. The ward then switched to softer alarms, rubber wheels and a rule for quiet talk after ten. Patients now report better sleep, and several recover a day sooner than expected.
options: Patients who sleep well are discharged a day early in most wards.
A nurse measured the noise but the ward changed nothing.
Reducing ward noise helped patients rest and recover.
Softer alarms were the main change made on the fourth floor.
quests.correctAnswer: Reducing ward noise helped patients rest and recover.
quests.hint: Sort the paragraph into problem, measurement, action and result.
quests.explanation: Noise was measured, reduced and linked to improved sleep and recovery. The wrong options deny any action, narrow the changes to one or turn 'several' into 'always'.
keyPoints: Noise on a hospital ward disturbed patients' sleep.
A nurse's measurements led to softer alarms, rubber wheels and quiet rules.
Patients sleep better and some recover sooner.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A grocery co-operative opened in a neighbourhood that had no supermarket for years. Residents each paid a small share and now vote on what the store stocks. The shelves lean toward local produce, and prices are slightly higher than at chain stores. Even so, membership has grown every month. Members say they would rather pay a little more for a shop that listens to them and keeps money in the area.
options: The co-operative is popular because its prices are lower than chains.
A co-operative grocery succeeds through ownership and local benefit.
Residents opened the store after a supermarket closed nearby.
Members pay shares, but staff decide what is sold with little consultation.
quests.correctAnswer: A co-operative grocery succeeds through ownership and local benefit.
quests.hint: Notice which disadvantage the paragraph admits, and what outweighs it.
quests.explanation: Prices are higher, yet membership grows because people value a say and local benefit. The wrong options reverse the price comparison, change the store's history or deny members' vote.
keyPoints: A co-operative grocery opened where there had been no supermarket.
Members own shares and vote on stock, mostly local produce.
Prices are slightly higher, but membership keeps growing.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Many people believe reading on paper is always better for understanding, and bookshops often say so. Studies, however, show a rather more nuanced picture than that. Readers tend to skim on screens, which hurts comprehension of long, complex texts. For short, simple material, though, the difference nearly disappears. Some researchers add that readers who slow down and avoid distractions on a screen can understand nearly as well as on paper.
options: Paper beats screens in the studies for both short and long texts.
Researchers advise readers to skim long texts on screens.
Screens work as well as paper for long, complex texts.
Screen reading can match paper if readers slow down.
quests.correctAnswer: Screen reading can match paper if readers slow down.
quests.hint: Test each option for the words 'every' and 'always', which the paragraph avoids.
quests.explanation: The paragraph rejects the simple belief that paper always wins, showing that the difference depends on text type and reading habits. The wrong options swap one absolute claim for another.
keyPoints: Many people think paper always helps understanding more.
Screen readers skim, which harms understanding of long complex texts.
The gap shrinks for short texts or when readers slow down.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A secondary school asked students to hand in their phones at the start of each day. Teachers expected complaints, and there were a few in the first week. Yet by the end of the term, students were talking more at lunch and finishing more classwork. Bullying reports online also dropped slightly. Some parents still worry about not reaching their children in an emergency, so the school added a phone at the office.
options: A phone collection policy improved school life.
Parents demanded that the office phone be removed.
Students complained throughout the entire term about the policy.
The school banned students from owning phones at home.
quests.correctAnswer: A phone collection policy improved school life.
quests.hint: Include the benefit and the response to the remaining concern.
quests.explanation: Students benefited socially and academically, and the office phone answered parents' emergency worries. The wrong options extend the ban to home, reverse the reaction or invent a demand.
keyPoints: A school collects phones from students each morning.
Students talk more, finish more work and bully less online.
An office phone reassures parents about emergencies.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: The council dimmed street lights between midnight and five to save electricity. Some residents feared crime would rise, so police tracked incidents for a year. Burglaries did not increase, and traffic accidents at night remained level. The energy bill fell by a quarter, and astronomers noticed that stars were more visible above the town. The council now plans to dim the lights on the ring road as well.
options: The council has already dimmed the ring road's lights.
Astronomers asked the council to switch the lights off after midnight.
Dimming street lights saved energy without more crime.
Police recorded more burglaries once the lights were dimmed.
quests.correctAnswer: Dimming street lights saved energy without more crime.
quests.hint: Keep the worry, the evidence and the result together.
quests.explanation: The council's test showed savings and no extra crime, so it plans more dimming. The wrong options reverse the crime data, treat a plan as completed or invent a request.
keyPoints: Street lights are dimmed from midnight to five to save power.
Police found no rise in burglaries or accidents.
The energy bill fell, and the ring road is next.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: In the border town's primary school, half the day is taught in Spanish and half in English. Teachers worried that children would fall behind in reading. Instead, test scores after three years were slightly above the regional average. Parents say the children switch easily between languages at home and are more confident with visitors. However, the school struggles to find enough teachers who are fully fluent in both languages.
options: The school teaches in Spanish for the first half of the year and English after.
Bilingual teaching is working well, though finding fluent teachers is difficult.
Parents complain that visitors are not confident with children.
Children in the school fell behind in reading after three years.
quests.correctAnswer: Bilingual teaching is working well, though finding fluent teachers is difficult.
quests.hint: Include the success and the difficulty the school still faces.
quests.explanation: Results were positive, but recruitment is a problem. The wrong options reverse the reading outcome, misread the timetable or twist parents' comments.
keyPoints: The border-town school teaches half in Spanish and half in English.
After three years, scores are slightly above average and children are confident.
Fluent bilingual teachers are hard to find.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: At the library, a weekly class helps people over sixty to use smartphones. Volunteers begin with basics such as answering calls and sending photos. Students then move on to video calls and online banking, often bringing their own phones to practise. Many say their main motivation is seeing grandchildren who live far away. The librarian adds that the class has become as much a social club as a lesson.
options: Volunteers teach basic calls and photos, and learners stop there.
The class is for young people who want to bank online.
A phone class for older adults teaches skills and builds friendships.
Students attend mainly to earn a certificate in technology.
quests.correctAnswer: A phone class for older adults teaches skills and builds friendships.
quests.hint: Watch for options that stop at the first step of the course.
quests.explanation: The class moves from basics to advanced skills, driven by family contact, and it also creates social connection. The wrong options change the audience, limit the content or replace the motivation.
keyPoints: The library runs a weekly smartphone class for people over sixty.
Learners progress from calls and photos to video calls and banking.
Seeing far-away grandchildren motivates them, and the class is also social.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Rural households often have slow internet, which makes online work and study difficult. A village cooperative decided to lay its own fibre cable rather than wait for a commercial provider. Members dug the trenches themselves to reduce costs. After eighteen months, every home was connected at speeds ten times faster than before. Neighbouring villages have asked for advice about copying the model.
options: A village built its own fast internet network.
A commercial provider connected the village after eighteen months.
Members paid contractors to dig trenches for the cable.
Neighbouring villages have already built their own networks.
quests.correctAnswer: A village built its own fast internet network.
quests.hint: Compare what the village chose to do with what it might have done.
quests.explanation: The village acted itself instead of waiting, saved money by digging trenches and now advises others. The wrong options reverse who built the network, how costs were reduced and the neighbours' stage.
keyPoints: Slow rural internet made online work and study hard.
A cooperative laid its own fibre cable and dug the trenches.
Homes now have much faster connections, and other villages want advice.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: In the mountain district, most firefighters are volunteers who leave their jobs when the siren sounds. Employers must accept that some workers will disappear for hours. Many are supportive, but a few resent the disruption. The fire service is now offering small tax breaks to companies that release volunteers without penalty. Officials say the district cannot afford to pay a full-time force, so the arrangement is vital.
options: Employers resent volunteers leaving work, and refuse tax breaks for that reason.
Volunteer firefighters need employer support, so incentives exist.
Volunteers are paid tax breaks when they respond.
The district can afford a full-time fire force.
quests.correctAnswer: Volunteer firefighters need employer support, so incentives exist.
quests.hint: Ask who the incentive is for and why it is needed.
quests.explanation: The system relies on employers' cooperation, which the tax breaks encourage. The wrong options reverse the funding statement, exaggerate resentment or redirect the incentive.
keyPoints: Most mountain firefighters are volunteers with other jobs.
Some employers dislike the disruption when volunteers leave.
Tax breaks aim to keep employers supportive because a paid force is unaffordable.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A hospital canteen replaced sweets in its vending machines with fruit, nuts and yoghurt. Sales dropped for the first month, and some staff grumbled. Then the hospital gave discounts on healthy items and moved them to eye level. Within three months, revenue had recovered and staff members were asking for more choice. A survey showed that fewer employees felt sleepy in the afternoon.
options: Healthier vending worked once it was easier and cheaper.
Vending sales stayed high throughout the first month.
The hospital banned staff from buying sweets anywhere.
Staff asked the canteen to bring back the sweets.
quests.correctAnswer: Healthier vending worked once it was easier and cheaper.
quests.hint: Track how the first reaction differs from the later result.
quests.explanation: Sales initially fell, but discounts and placement changed behaviour, with benefits noted later. The wrong options deny the dip, extend the policy or reverse the staff's request.
keyPoints: The hospital swapped sweets for healthier snacks in vending machines.
Sales dipped at first, then discounts and eye-level placement helped.
Revenue recovered, and staff felt less sleepy.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A nightclub near the river received repeated noise complaints from new apartment residents. The club had been there for twenty years, and its owner felt it was unfair to blame him. After mediation, the club installed sound-absorbing panels and closed the courtyard at midnight. Complaints fell sharply, though one resident still says the bass can be heard on quiet nights. The owner says the panels cost him less than a lawsuit would have.
options: The owner paid more for panels than for a lawsuit.
The club was forced to close after twenty years.
Mediation led a nightclub to cut its noise.
Residents stopped complaining once the courtyard closed, and the owner sold up.
quests.correctAnswer: Mediation led a nightclub to cut its noise.
quests.hint: Include the compromise and the remaining complaint.
quests.explanation: The club and residents reached a workable solution, though not a perfect one. The wrong options exaggerate the outcome, deny the remaining complaint or reverse the cost comparison.
keyPoints: New residents complained about noise from a long-established nightclub.
Mediation produced panels and an earlier courtyard closing.
Complaints fell, though one resident still hears the bass.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: The construction industry faces a shortage of skilled bricklayers. Many experienced workers are retiring, and few young people are training to replace them. Firms are offering higher pay, but that has not solved the problem. Some are now recruiting from abroad, while colleges are trying to make the trade look more attractive. Analysts say no single measure will fill the gap quickly.
options: Young people are training in large numbers to become bricklayers.
Higher pay has solved the bricklayer shortage.
Analysts believe recruiting from abroad will fix the shortage quickly.
Bricklayer shortages persist despite higher pay.
quests.correctAnswer: Bricklayer shortages persist despite higher pay.
quests.hint: Check whether an option says a measure worked when the paragraph says it did not.
quests.explanation: Pay rises alone did not close the gap, and other responses are underway with no quick fix. The wrong options claim success or overstate one solution.
keyPoints: Experienced bricklayers are retiring, and few young people replace them.
Higher pay, foreign recruitment and college campaigns are being tried.
Analysts say no single measure will quickly fill the gap.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Video interviews save time for both companies and candidates. However, recruiters admit that poor lighting or a weak connection can distract from a candidate's ability. Some firms now allow applicants to reschedule if their connection fails. Others ask candidates to record answers in advance, so they can choose their own time. Critics say this shifts pressure onto candidates who must perform without any human response.
options: Video interviews have removed the technical problems from recruiting.
Firms have dropped live interviews in favour of recorded answers across the sector.
Video interviews save time and create new pressures.
Critics say recorded answers make interviews less stressful.
quests.correctAnswer: Video interviews save time and create new pressures.
quests.hint: Balance the advantages against the drawbacks the writer lists.
quests.explanation: The paragraph shows convenience alongside technical and psychological concerns and different company responses. The wrong options overstate success, turn 'others' into 'all' or reverse critics' claim.
keyPoints: Video interviews save time for firms and candidates.
Poor lighting or connections can hide a candidate's real ability.
Rescheduling and recorded answers help some but create pressure for others.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A bakery chain decided to buy its flour from mills within a hundred kilometres. Delivery costs dropped, and the flour arrived fresher. However, harvests vary between regions, so quality changed from month to month. The chain solved this by mixing local flours and testing each batch. Customers cannot taste much difference, but the company now advertises its local sourcing, and sales have risen slightly.
options: Local flour brought savings, and quality needed managing.
Customers said local bread tastes much better than before.
The chain stopped testing flour after it went local.
Delivery costs rose because of the shorter distances.
quests.correctAnswer: Local flour brought savings, and quality needed managing.
quests.hint: Look for the benefit, the complication and how it was handled.
quests.explanation: Local sourcing helped costs and freshness, created a quality problem and was managed through blending and testing. The wrong options reverse the testing, exaggerate taste and reverse costs.
keyPoints: A bakery chain buys flour from mills within a hundred kilometres.
Harvest differences caused variation, so it mixes and tests batches.
Customers notice little difference, but local sourcing helps sales.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A fashion rental service lets customers borrow party clothes for a few days instead of buying them. Many people wear an outfit only once, so renting seems sensible. The service says each garment is worn about thirty times before retirement. Critics point out that shipping and cleaning use energy, and that rentals may encourage people to wear more outfits. The environmental benefit, they conclude, depends on how the service is run.
options: Critics say the service uses little energy for cleaning and shipping.
Each garment is retired after a single rental, which is why critics object.
Clothing rental's benefit depends on how it operates.
Renting clothes is better for the environment than buying, in the critics' view.
quests.correctAnswer: Clothing rental's benefit depends on how it operates.
quests.hint: Give attention to the conclusion critics draw at the end.
quests.explanation: The service saves clothes from being worn once, but transport and cleaning may cancel benefits, so the outcome is conditional. The wrong options claim it is always better, reverse the lifespan or deny energy use.
keyPoints: Customers rent party outfits that they might only wear once.
Garments are worn around thirty times before retiring.
Shipping, cleaning and extra outfits mean the benefit depends on how it is run.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia does not rely on tablets. Patients keep a sleep diary and set a fixed wake-up time, even after a poor night. They also learn to leave the bed when they cannot sleep, so the bed is linked with rest rather than worry. The first weeks can feel harder because sleep time is limited on purpose. After two months, most patients fall asleep faster and wake less often.
options: The first weeks of therapy are easier than the later weeks.
Patients are told to stay in bed when they cannot sleep.
Insomnia therapy depends mainly on taking tablets before bed.
Behavioural therapy improves insomnia but is hard initially.
quests.correctAnswer: Behavioural therapy improves insomnia but is hard initially.
quests.hint: Include both the method and the difficulty at the start.
quests.explanation: The therapy relies on routine and reassociation, with an initial dip before improvement. The wrong options reverse the medication, bed rules and time course.
keyPoints: This therapy for insomnia avoids tablets.
Patients keep diaries, wake at fixed times and leave bed when awake.
It is harder at first but usually improves sleep within two months.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Runners often increase their weekly distance too quickly and then suffer injuries. Physiotherapists recommend adding no more than ten percent each week. They also suggest one lighter week out of every four, so the body can adapt. Beginners who follow these limits tend to stay injury-free longer. Experienced runners sometimes ignore the advice, believing their fitness protects them, yet they are frequently the ones who end up in the clinic.
options: Physiotherapists recommend increasing distance by ten percent daily.
Gradual increases and rest weeks help runners avoid injuries.
Beginners get hurt more often when they follow the limits.
Experienced runners are the least likely to be injured.
quests.correctAnswer: Gradual increases and rest weeks help runners avoid injuries.
quests.hint: Note the advice, then check who ignores it and what happens.
quests.explanation: The advice is to increase gradually and rest, and experienced runners who ignore it often get injured. The wrong options reverse who is injured, the time period and the effect on beginners.
keyPoints: Runners often add distance too fast and get injured.
Physiotherapists suggest a ten-percent weekly limit and easier weeks.
Ignoring the advice often sends experienced runners to the clinic.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: When the city introduced water meters, households began paying for what they used. Some families worried about higher bills, but average consumption fell by fifteen percent within a year. Leaks were repaired faster because people noticed rising figures. Poorer households received a small discount to protect them from hardship. The utility says the savings have delayed the need for a new reservoir.
options: Meters increased water use by fifteen percent within a year.
Water meters encouraged conservation while protecting low-income households.
Poorer households were charged more than wealthier ones.
The utility has already built a new reservoir.
quests.correctAnswer: Water meters encouraged conservation while protecting low-income households.
quests.hint: Connect the change in payment to the change in behaviour.
quests.explanation: Paying by use reduced consumption and repaired leaks, with a discount for poorer households and a delay to a costly project. The wrong options reverse the use trend, treat a delay as a construction or reverse the discount.
keyPoints: Households pay for the water they use after meters were installed.
Consumption fell fifteen percent, and leaks were fixed sooner.
Poorer households get a discount, and a new reservoir can wait.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Volunteers spent a Saturday cleaning a stretch of river near the old mill. They pulled out tyres, bottles and a rusted bicycle. The team then tested the water and found it cleaner than expected. This surprised them, because they had assumed the rubbish would harm water quality. A local biologist explained that the river's fast flow dilutes pollution, but she warned that rubbish still harms fish and birds.
options: The team found the water badly polluted by the rubbish.
The biologist said rubbish poses little threat to fish and birds.
Volunteers were disappointed that they found little rubbish along the river.
A river clean-up showed cleaner water than expected.
quests.correctAnswer: A river clean-up showed cleaner water than expected.
quests.hint: Include the surprise and the biologist's warning.
quests.explanation: The result contradicted an assumption, but the biologist noted that rubbish is still harmful in other ways. The wrong options reverse the water finding, the rubbish finding or the warning.
keyPoints: Volunteers removed tyres, bottles and a bicycle from a river.
Testing showed cleaner water than they expected.
A biologist said fast flow dilutes pollution, but rubbish still harms wildlife.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: The lighthouse on the northern point was automated fifty years ago, and the keepers' cottages fell empty. A trust now rents the cottages to visitors and offers guided tours of the tower. Bookings in summer are full, and the income funds repairs to the lamp room. Locals say they are glad to see the building alive again, though some feel the narrow road is too crowded on weekends. Sailors passing at night still see its lamp turn, which many find comforting.
options: Tourism has revived a lighthouse and funds its repairs.
Income from visitors is spent on widening the road.
The lighthouse still employs keepers who live in the cottages.
Locals want the lighthouse to close to visitors.
quests.correctAnswer: Tourism has revived a lighthouse and funds its repairs.
quests.hint: Watch how the use of the building has changed over fifty years.
quests.explanation: A once-empty site now earns money for its maintenance, with a downside for locals. The wrong options reverse the keepers' status, locals' opinion or the use of income.
keyPoints: The lighthouse was automated and its cottages were emptied.
A trust rents the cottages and runs tours, funding repairs.
Locals like the revival, but weekend traffic is a problem.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Museums are experimenting with audio guides that respond to where a visitor stands. Sensors detect the room, and the guide offers a short story about the nearest object. Visitors like not having to type numbers, and they spend longer in each gallery. However, some say the constant commentary makes it hard to talk with friends. One museum now lets visitors switch to a silent mode that shows text on a small screen.
options: Visitors must type numbers to hear each story.
The silent mode plays commentary through headphones.
Location-aware guides engage visitors and interrupt conversation.
Museums have replaced human guides with sensors in the galleries.
quests.correctAnswer: Location-aware guides engage visitors and interrupt conversation.
quests.hint: Include the appeal of the technology and the objection to it.
quests.explanation: The guides improve engagement but interrupt conversation, prompting a text-based alternative. The wrong options reverse the interface, exaggerate replacement or misstate what silent mode does.
keyPoints: Audio guides play stories triggered by the visitor's location.
Visitors spend more time in galleries and avoid typing numbers.
Because commentary interrupts talking, one museum added a silent text mode.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A radio station in the coastal town began broadcasting local podcasts in the evenings. Residents record short stories about the neighbourhood, from fishing memories to school days. The station says listeners in their eighties phone in to add details. Younger people enjoy hearing the town as it used to be. A university student is now collecting the recordings into an archive so they will not be lost.
options: The radio station charges residents to record their stories.
Local podcasts preserve residents' memories.
The university student has finished building the archive.
Younger people avoid the evening podcasts because the stories are about the past.
quests.correctAnswer: Local podcasts preserve residents' memories.
quests.hint: Think about who speaks, who listens and what is being preserved.
quests.explanation: The programme links generations through recorded memories, and an archive is being compiled. The wrong options add a fee, limit the audience or treat ongoing work as done.
keyPoints: A coastal radio station airs residents' recorded local stories.
Older listeners add details, and younger people enjoy the past.
A student is collecting the recordings into an archive.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Some schools have stopped teaching cursive handwriting, arguing that typing is more useful. Yet research suggests that writing by hand helps young children learn letter shapes and spelling. Students who take notes by hand also tend to process ideas more deeply, since they cannot write everything down. Typing has its own advantages, such as speed and easy editing. Many teachers now aim for a mix instead of choosing one method.
options: Students who write by hand record everything the teacher says.
Schools that stopped cursive have proven that typing is better.
Research shows that typing teaches letter shapes better than handwriting.
Handwriting and typing each help, so teachers combine them.
quests.correctAnswer: Handwriting and typing each help, so teachers combine them.
quests.hint: Decide whether the writer picks a winner or recommends balance.
quests.explanation: Each method has strengths, so a mix is preferred. The wrong options reverse the research, treat a policy as proof or reverse the note-taking finding.
keyPoints: Some schools dropped cursive because typing seems more useful.
Handwriting helps young children learn letters and process notes deeply.
Typing offers speed, so many teachers use both.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: The regional orchestra relies on ticket sales for only a third of its income. Sponsors and grants cover the rest, which makes it vulnerable when the economy weakens. Recently, a major sponsor withdrew, and the orchestra had to cancel two concerts. Musicians launched a campaign asking each audience member to bring one new person to the next performance. They hope a wider audience will attract new supporters as well as ticket buyers.
options: Ticket sales cover most of the orchestra's income.
An orchestra facing lost funding seeks a wider audience.
Musicians cancelled concerts to save money on sponsors.
Audience members are asked to pay a second ticket price.
quests.correctAnswer: An orchestra facing lost funding seeks a wider audience.
quests.hint: Follow the chain from vulnerability to problem to response.
quests.explanation: The orchestra depends on outside money, lost a sponsor and is trying to broaden its audience. The wrong options reverse income sources, the reason for cancellation or the campaign request.
keyPoints: Ticket sales provide only a third of the orchestra's income.
A sponsor left, and two concerts were cancelled.
Musicians ask audience members to bring someone new.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Shared bicycles were introduced in the city last year, and they were quickly vandalised. Repair costs soared, and the company almost withdrew. It then added GPS trackers and a rule that riders must park in marked bays. Damage fell by two thirds, and the bikes are now used ten thousand times a day. The city hopes to double the fleet once the numbers remain stable through winter.
options: The city has already doubled the fleet of bikes.
The company withdrew the bikes after they were vandalised.
Trackers and parking rules reduced bike vandalism.
Damage to the bikes increased after the trackers were added.
quests.correctAnswer: Trackers and parking rules reduced bike vandalism.
quests.hint: Separate what happened from what the city is still waiting to see.
quests.explanation: The company answered vandalism with tracking and rules, and the result was a big drop in damage. The wrong options reverse the outcome or treat a hope as done.
keyPoints: Shared bikes were quickly vandalised, and repair costs soared.
The company added trackers and required parking in bays.
Damage fell by two thirds, and the city hopes to expand.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Under the new tenancy law, landlords must give sixty days' notice before ending a lease, unless a tenant has broken the agreement. Tenants' groups welcomed the change because sudden evictions used to leave families scrambling. Landlords argue that the law makes it harder to sell property. A recent survey found that most tenants feel more secure, while small landlords are anxious about delays. Lawmakers say they will review the law after two years.
options: A tenancy law gave renters security and worried landlords.
Tenants' groups opposed the change because it slowed evictions.
Landlords can now end leases at short notice, unless a tenant has paid in advance.
Lawmakers have already cancelled the new law.
quests.correctAnswer: A tenancy law gave renters security and worried landlords.
quests.hint: Give both groups' viewpoints and the plan for review.
quests.explanation: The law protects tenants but troubles some landlords, and lawmakers plan a review. The wrong options reverse the notice rule, tenants' response or the law's status.
keyPoints: Landlords must now give sixty days' notice before ending a lease.
Tenants feel more secure, while small landlords worry about delays.
Lawmakers will review the law after two years.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: On the coast, farmers have begun growing seaweed on ropes in shallow water. The plants absorb carbon and nitrogen from the sea, and they need no fresh water or fertiliser. A small crop can be dried and sold as a food ingredient. But growing requires calm bays and permission from harbour authorities, which limits where farms can be built. Investors are interested, though they admit the market for seaweed is still small.
options: Investors say the market for seaweed is already large.
Seaweed can be grown in open water off the coast without a permit.
Seaweed farming is promising and limited by space and markets.
Seaweed farms need fresh water and fertiliser in order to grow.
quests.correctAnswer: Seaweed farming is promising and limited by space and markets.
quests.hint: Include the promise and the two restrictions the writer mentions.
quests.explanation: Seaweed offers benefits but faces space, permission and market limits. The wrong options reverse the water need, the permission rule or the market size.
keyPoints: Farmers grow seaweed on ropes in shallow sea water.
It absorbs carbon and nitrogen and needs no fertiliser.
Calm bays, permits and a small market limit growth.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A train operator introduced quiet carriages, where phone calls and loud music are not allowed. Commuters who work on laptops liked the change. Parents with young children, however, felt uncomfortable and sometimes moved elsewhere. Staff say enforcing the rule is difficult because the sign is easy to overlook. The operator is now testing bright floor markings and announcements before each departure, hoping that passengers will notice the rule.
options: Quiet carriages help some passengers and are hard to enforce.
Parents with young children prefer the quiet carriages on trains.
Staff find it easy to enforce the quiet rule.
The operator has removed the quiet carriages after complaints.
quests.correctAnswer: Quiet carriages help some passengers and are hard to enforce.
quests.hint: Give the benefit, the group it affects and the practical problem.
quests.explanation: Some commuters gain, some parents feel excluded, and enforcement requires better signage. The wrong options reverse parents' preference, enforcement ease or the scheme's status.
keyPoints: Quiet carriages ban calls and loud music.
Laptop workers like them, but parents with children feel uneasy.
Enforcement is hard, so markings and announcements are being tested.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: In many communities, groups of friends form a lending circle: each member contributes a fixed amount every month, and one person receives the full pot in turn. The system needs no bank and charges no interest. It works because members trust each other and would be ashamed to let the group down. Financial advisers point out that there is no protection if someone stops paying. Even so, millions of people rely on such circles worldwide.
options: Banks guarantee that members will be paid if someone stops contributing.
Lending circles charge high interest to members who receive the pot late.
Advisers recommend lending circles as the safest financial choice.
Lending circles work through trust, despite lacking formal protection.
quests.correctAnswer: Lending circles work through trust, despite lacking formal protection.
quests.hint: Find what makes the system function and what it lacks.
quests.explanation: The circle depends on trust and social pressure, and the lack of protection is an acknowledged weakness. The wrong options say there is interest, a bank guarantee or an adviser endorsement.
keyPoints: Members contribute monthly, and each takes a turn receiving the pot.
No bank or interest is involved because trust holds it together.
There is no protection if someone stops paying, yet millions use them.
